title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every subarray directly versus tracking a running max and min together.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums of integers, find a contiguous subarray whose product is the largest among all possible contiguous subarrays, and return that largest product.

blocks.text: Given an array nums of integers, find a contiguous subarray whose product is the largest among all possible contiguous subarrays, and return that largest product.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Chain of Multipliers That Can Flip Sign
blocks.text: Like a chain of gain and loss multipliers where a negative multiplier does not just reduce the total, it flips whatever has been building up from a loss into a gain, or from a gain into a loss, which means the best chain so far is not always the one that looks best right now.

blocks.text: Taking the whole array multiplies two negative numbers together, flipping the sign back to positive: -2 times 3 times -4 equals 24, larger than any shorter subarray.
It is worth asking why a technique that tracks just one running value, the way it does for a running sum or a running minimum price, is not enough here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock showed the power of tracking a single running extreme value in one pass, there a running minimum, to avoid rescanning the array.

Observation 2: A first instinct might be to track only a running maximum product ending at each position, the way a running sum based approach would. But multiplying by a negative number does not just shrink a running value, it can flip its sign entirely.

Observation 3: That means the most negative running product ending at a position is just as dangerous, or valuable, as the most positive one, since multiplying it by another negative number can vault it straight to the new best.

Observation 4: Tracking both a running maximum and a running minimum ending at each position, and swapping the two before extending them whenever the current number is negative, correctly captures both possibilities in a single pass, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [2, 3, -2, 4] through to its correct answer, 6.

Recognizing that multiplication by a negative number can flip which running value is "best" is what motivates tracking a running minimum alongside the running maximum, rather than just one running value.
Check every possible contiguous subarray, computing its product directly, and keep track of the largest product found.

items: For every starting index i, start a running product at 1.
Extend the subarray one element at a time to every ending index j, multiplying the running product by nums[j].
Keep the largest product seen across every subarray.

codes.python:
def max_product(nums):
    best = nums[0]
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):                                      # every possible starting index
        product = 1
        for j in range(i, n):                                 # extend the subarray one step at a time
            product *= nums[j]
            best = max(best, product)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [2, 3, -2, 4]
    print(max_product(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible starting index is tried, and for each one, the subarray is extended one element at a time, recomputing the product as it grows.
A long running product is used in the Java and C++ versions to avoid overflow while accumulating, only narrowed to a 32 bit int when comparing against best.
This approach checks every subarray directly, so it correctly handles sign flips, but it does not yet expose any structure to solve the problem faster.

blocks.text: Every contiguous subarray is directly checked, so the true maximum product is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for every pair of start and end indices.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.

Limitation: this does not use any structure to avoid recomputation, and does not yet expose the actual difficulty of this problem, which is handling negative numbers whose product with another negative number can suddenly become the new best.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: recomputing the product from scratch for every start and end index pair repeats almost all of the same multiplications many times over.

What a single running maximum, Kadane style, would normally fix: extend a running best product ending at the current position instead of recomputing from every start index.

Why a running maximum alone is not sufficient here: a negative current number multiplied against a very negative running minimum can produce a large positive product, one a running maximum alone would never have kept around.

The core idea: track both a running maximum and a running minimum ending at the current position, swap the two whenever the current number is negative, and then extend each with the current value, or restart at the current value if that is larger.

Walk through the array once, but keep track of two running values ending at the current position, not just one: the maximum product so far, and the minimum product so far. A negative current number can turn the smallest running product (likely negative) into the largest one, and vice versa, so both must be tracked and possibly swapped before extending them with the current value.
Track both a running maximum and a running minimum product ending at each position, since a negative number can flip which one becomes the new best.

blocks.caption: Optimized: track both a running max and a running min, since a negative flips them

codes.python:
def max_product(nums):
    max_ending = nums[0]
    min_ending = nums[0]
    best = nums[0]
    for num in nums[1:]:
        if num < 0:
            max_ending, min_ending = min_ending, max_ending           # a negative number swaps which is which
        max_ending = max(num, max_ending * num)
        min_ending = min(num, min_ending * num)
        best = max(best, max_ending)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [2, 3, -2, 4]
    print(max_product(nums))

blocks.text: This works because swapping the running maximum and minimum before applying a negative number correctly anticipates the sign flip: the previous running minimum, likely a large negative number, becomes the candidate for the new maximum once multiplied by another negative, and the previous running maximum becomes the candidate for the new minimum.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per element.
Space: O(1), only a few running values are kept.

blocks.text: This is a variant of the running maximum subarray pattern, but the twist of tracking a running minimum alongside the running maximum, purely to handle the sign flipping behavior of negative numbers, is the key insight that separates this from a plain Kadane style sum problem.

items: Tracking only a running maximum, the way sum based subarray problems do, which silently produces wrong answers whenever two negative numbers should combine into a large positive product.
Forgetting to swap the running maximum and minimum before extending them when the current number is negative.

blocks.text: Walk through a small example with two negative numbers out loud, showing explicitly how the running minimum becomes the new running maximum, since this is the detail interviewers most want to see reasoned through.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "why not just track a running maximum like for sums", think: a negative number can flip a very negative running minimum into the new largest product.
If the interviewer says "what happens with a zero in the array", think: both running values reset to the current element, splitting the array into independent segments.
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra arrays", think: only three running variables, max ending here, min ending here, and best overall, are ever needed.

Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, whose single running extreme value in one pass is the simpler ancestor of tracking two running extremes here.
Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum, whose single running maximum and restart logic is directly extended here with a paired running minimum.
Any problem where an operation can flip sign or reverse an ordering (multiplication by a negative, for instance), where tracking both extremes together, not just one, is often required.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: a Kadane style single pass, but tracking both a running maximum and a running minimum ending at each position.

Core Idea: a negative number can flip the most negative running product into the largest one, so swapping the running maximum and minimum before extending them on a negative number correctly captures every possible sign flip in a single pass.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: multiplication, unlike addition, can flip sign, so the smallest running value matters just as much as the largest one.
Interview Difficulty: stating the single running maximum idea is easy; recognizing and correctly handling the sign flip with a paired running minimum is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: track the max and the min together, and swap them whenever a negative number shows up.
